restatements.text: Caps annual rent increases at 5 percent for residential units, but exempts units that were first occupied within the past 15 years.

findings.mechanism: Protects renters in applicable units from large rent spikes by setting a maximum allowable annual increase.

analysis.answer: Current law allows landlords to raise rent by any amount with 60 days' written notice. The measure changes this by capping rent increases at 5% within any 12-month period for units that have been occupied for more than 15 years.
Landlords of units older than 15 years face an opportunity cost of forgone rental income if market rent rates rise faster than 5% annually.

Renters in units older than 15 years benefit from capped rent increases and more predictable housing costs. Landlords of these units bear the cost of limited revenue growth. Renters and landlords in newer units are unaffected.

Landlords of regulated units might be incentivized to increase rents by the maximum 5% every year rather than sporadically, to avoid falling behind market rates. Some may reduce property maintenance to offset restricted revenue or attempt to convert rental units to for-sale properties. The 15-year rolling exemption aims to preserve developers' incentives to build new housing, though some might fear future regulatory expansions.

The measure addresses the problem of renters facing sudden, unaffordable rent spikes, using a 5% cap to prevent them. It includes a 15-year exemption for new units to prevent the rent cap from discouraging new housing construction.
Renters in older buildings gain more predictability over their housing costs, while landlords of those buildings lose discretion over their pricing.

The long-term effects of rent control are empirically disputed. Some research finds it successfully prevents displacement, providing stability for current tenants. Other research finds it reduces the overall quality and quantity of rental housing, as landlords may convert units to condos or under-maintain them, potentially driving up rents in the unregulated market.
The text does not specify an enforcement mechanism, so enforcement would likely rely on existing tenant-landlord civil court processes.
